title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
claim: Benchmark scores can mislead when the benchmark's difficulty weighting differs from the target, or when it leaves difficulty regions uncovered.
layout: 2 panels split by dashed line; curve above histograms, callout boxes at right
description: Two panels separated by a vertical dashed line, titled (a) Measure Mismatch and (b) Coverage Gaps. Both share a 'Question Difficulty' x-axis from Easy to Hard. Each has a performance-vs-difficulty curve on top and histograms of question density below. In (a), the blue Model A and orange Model B curves overlap on easy questions and split on hard ones. Beneath them are a blue benchmark histogram skewed easy and an orange histogram of interest skewed hard. Callout boxes show the benchmark scores (A=72.1, B=72.4, 'Indistinguishable!') against the target scores (A=61.8, B=68.9, 'Clear difference!'). In (b), grey Before Training and blue After Training curves differ only in a green-shaded region. The benchmark histogram has no bars there. A box notes that the observed score barely moves (64.2 to 64.6), so training progress is missed. Green italic annotations mark the gap.
caption: Two benchmark failure cases. In both panels, the curves show true model conditional performance as a function of question difficulty. (a) Measure Mismatch. The benchmark emphasizes easy questions, where the models perform similarly, while the difficulty distribution we care about places more weight on harder questions, where they differ substantially. Because the benchmark and the target distribution weight the difficulty axis differently, they lead to different conclusions for the same two models. (b) Coverage Gaps. A model actually improves substantially over a localized difficulty region. Because the benchmark has no questions in that region, this improvement is not reflected in the observed benchmark score, causing meaningful training progress to be missed.
abstract: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.
